subject: chemistry
topicDisplay: Production, use and disposal of important chemicals and materials
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on the Haber process, yield, atom economy and life cycle assessment, then mark my answer against the Eduqas spec.
promptWeak: Explain the Haber process, percentage yield, atom economy, corrosion and life cycle assessment for GCSE Eduqas Chemistry simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: What is manufactured in the Haber process, and why is it important in agriculture?
options: Sulfuric acid, used to treat soil
Oxygen, used to help crops respire
Carbon dioxide, used to feed plants
Ammonia, used to make nitrogen-based fertilisers
questions.explain: The Haber process makes ammonia (NH3) from nitrogen and hydrogen. Ammonia is used to make nitrogenous fertilisers that increase crop yields.

questions.q: What are the raw materials that provide the nitrogen and hydrogen for the Haber process?
options: Nitrogen from the air and hydrogen from natural gas
Nitrogen from limestone and hydrogen from water only
Nitrogen from ammonia and hydrogen from air
Nitrogen from crude oil and hydrogen from limestone
questions.explain: Nitrogen comes from the air and hydrogen is obtained mainly from natural gas (methane) reacting with steam.

questions.q: Which three elements are supplied by NPK fertilisers to help agricultural production?
options: Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
Sodium, chlorine and oxygen
Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen
Sodium, calcium and iron
questions.explain: NPK fertilisers provide nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K), the key nutrients for plant growth.

questions.q: What is a potential drawback of overusing nitrogen fertilisers?
options: Crops grow too slowly
The soil becomes too alkaline to test
Ammonia turns into oxygen
Fertiliser washes into rivers and can cause eutrophication
questions.explain: Overuse means excess fertiliser is washed into waterways, causing eutrophication (algal blooms then oxygen depletion), harming aquatic life.

questions.q: How can ammonia gas be identified?
options: It relights a glowing splint
It turns limewater milky
It turns damp red litmus paper blue
It gives a squeaky pop
questions.explain: Ammonia is alkaline, so it turns damp red litmus paper blue. It also has a characteristic sharp smell.

questions.q: How can you test a solid to show it contains ammonium ions?
options: Add barium chloride and look for a white precipitate
Add sodium hydroxide, warm, and test for ammonia gas released
Add dilute acid and test for carbon dioxide
Add silver nitrate and look for a cream precipitate
questions.explain: Warming an ammonium salt with sodium hydroxide releases ammonia gas, which turns damp red litmus paper blue, confirming ammonium ions.

questions.q: A graph shows the rate of an industrial reaction rising as temperature increases. What does this indicate about the operating conditions?
options: Higher temperature always lowers the rate
Temperature has no effect on rate
Rate only depends on the catalyst
Higher temperature increases the rate of reaction
questions.explain: Interpreting the graph, a higher temperature increases the rate of reaction because particles collide more often and with more energy.

questions.q: In the Haber process the forward reaction is exothermic. A moderate temperature of about 450 C is used rather than a very low temperature because:
options: A low temperature would increase both yield and rate
A low temperature gives a higher yield but too slow a rate, so a compromise is used
A high temperature always gives the maximum yield
Temperature has no effect on the equilibrium
questions.explain: A lower temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction (higher yield) but the rate becomes too slow. About 450 C is a compromise between acceptable yield and a fast enough rate.

questions.q: The Haber process uses a high pressure of around 200 atmospheres. Why is an even higher pressure not usually used?
options: Higher pressure would lower the yield
Very high pressures are expensive and dangerous to maintain
Pressure has no effect on the equilibrium
Higher pressure would stop the catalyst working permanently
questions.explain: Higher pressure does increase the yield of ammonia, but very high pressures require costly, strong equipment and raise safety risks, so a compromise pressure is chosen.

questions.q: How is percentage yield of a reaction calculated?
options: (theoretical yield / actual yield) x 100
actual yield x theoretical yield
theoretical yield - actual yield
(actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100
questions.explain: Percentage yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) x 100. It is always the actual divided by the theoretical.

questions.q: A reaction has a theoretical yield of 40 g but only 30 g of product is obtained. What is the percentage yield?
questions.explain: Percentage yield = (30 / 40) x 100 = 75%.

questions.q: What does the atom economy of a reaction measure?
options: The percentage of reactant atoms that end up in the desired product
The speed of the reaction
The cost of the reactants
The amount of catalyst needed
questions.explain: Atom economy is the proportion (percentage) of the mass of reactant atoms that become the useful desired product, showing how efficiently raw materials are used.

questions.q: A reaction produces 44 g of desired product from reactants with a total mass of 100 g. What is the atom economy?
questions.explain: Atom economy = (mass of desired product / total mass of reactants) x 100 = (44 / 100) x 100 = 44%.

questions.q: When choosing a reaction pathway to make a product, which combination of factors is most desirable?
options: Low yield, low atom economy, useless by-products
High yield, high atom economy, and useful by-products
High yield but no consideration of atom economy
Slow rate and expensive raw materials
questions.explain: A good pathway has a high yield, high atom economy, a suitable rate and equilibrium position, and any by-products that are themselves useful, reducing waste and cost.

questions.q: Which two substances must be present for iron to rust (corrode)?
options: Oxygen and water
Carbon dioxide and water
Nitrogen and oxygen
Water and salt only
questions.explain: Iron corrodes (rusts) when both oxygen and water are present. Salt speeds it up but is not essential.

questions.q: Galvanising coats iron with zinc. How does the zinc protect the iron even if the coating is scratched?
options: It makes the iron heavier
It removes all oxygen from the air
It turns the iron into an alloy of gold
It acts as a sacrificial metal, corroding in preference to the iron
questions.explain: Zinc is more reactive than iron, so it corrodes in preference to the iron (sacrificial protection) as well as forming a physical barrier to oxygen and water.

questions.q: Which statement comparing material properties is generally correct?
options: Ceramics such as glass and clay are typically hard but brittle
Polymers are always harder than metals
Composites are always weaker than their separate materials
Metals are usually brittle and non-conducting
questions.explain: Ceramics like glass and clay are hard but brittle. Metals are typically strong and malleable; composites combine materials to improve properties; polymers vary but are usually less hard than metals.

questions.q: What does a life cycle assessment (LCA) of a product consider?
options: Only the cost of the raw materials
Only how the product is advertised
The environmental impact at every stage, from raw materials to disposal
Only the energy used during manufacture
questions.explain: An LCA assesses the environmental impact across the whole life: obtaining raw materials, manufacture, use, and disposal (including whether it can be recycled).

questions.q: An LCA shows Material A uses less energy to make but cannot be recycled, while Material B uses more energy but is recyclable. What is the best conclusion?
options: Material A is always better because making it uses less energy
A judgement must weigh manufacturing energy against end-of-life impact such as recyclability
Material B is useless because it uses more energy
LCA data cannot be used to compare materials
questions.explain: Interpreting LCA data means weighing all stages: lower manufacturing energy must be balanced against the disposal impact, so recyclability of B may outweigh A's lower production energy.

questions.q: Which factor would most strongly support a decision to recycle a metal rather than extract new metal?
options: Recycling uses more energy and raw material
Recycling always produces a lower quality metal
Recycling releases more carbon dioxide than extraction
Recycling saves energy and conserves finite ore reserves
questions.explain: Recycling metals generally saves energy and conserves limited ore reserves, reducing environmental impact, which is a key factor favouring recycling.
